summary: Describes a standard method for storing Diffie-Hellman keys in the DNS using KEY resource records. It was later updated by RFC 6944.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to keep a public piece of a secret-code-agreement trick in the internet's phone book.

questions: how are diffie-hellman keys stored in dns
what are the well-known diffie-hellman groups in dns
why is there no sig record for diffie-hellman
subtitle: How DNS stores the public part of a Diffie-Hellman key in a KEY record, including two well-known prime groups.

tldr.problem: DNS could carry cryptographic keys, but there was no standard layout for publishing Diffie-Hellman keys, which two parties use to derive a shared secret.
tldr.mechanism: A Diffie-Hellman key is stored in a KEY record with algorithm number 2, holding the prime p, the generator g and the public value. A short index can stand in for two well-known prime/generator pairs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2539 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 6944. It defines no SIG record for Diffie-Hellman, and the usual Diffie-Hellman key strength rules still apply.

today: RFC 2539 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6944, so read the two together.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Keys in the DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) was extended in RFC 2535 to carry digital signatures and cryptographic keys, so it can be used for secure key distribution. RFC 2539 describes how to store Diffie-Hellman keys in the DNS, and assumes the reader knows the Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

Part of the format and its description came from a work in progress by Ashar Aziz, Tom Markson and Hemma Prafullchandra.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet's phone book can hold keys. This document says how to write down the public half of one special kind of key, the kind used to agree on a secret.

sections.title: How Diffie-Hellman Works Here
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman needs two parties to interact to derive keying information, which can then be used for authentication. Suppose they hold local secrets i and j and compute X = g^i (mod p) and Y = g^j (mod p). They swap X and Y, and each computes the same shared secret, Zi = Y^i (mod p) and Zj = X^j (mod p). An adversary who does not know i or j cannot learn it from the exchanged messages, unless the adversary can compute a discrete logarithm mod p, which is hard for strong p and g.

Each party's private key is its secret i (or j). The public key is the pair p and g, which must be the same for both parties, plus the party's own X (or Y).

Because DNS SIG records are mainly stored authenticators of zone data for many different resolvers, no Diffie-Hellman algorithm SIG record is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people each mix a private color into a shared public color and swap the mixes. Each then adds their own private color again and both end up with the same secret color that no onlooker can work out.

sections.title: The Diffie-Hellman KEY Record
sections.content:
Diffie-Hellman keys are KEY records with algorithm number 2. The first 4 octets (flags, protocol and algorithm) are common to all KEY records as described in RFC 2535. The rest, from prime length through the public value, is the public key part. The period of validity is not in the KEY record. It is shown by the SIG record that signs the KEY record at that domain name.

After the common fields come these, in order: prime length, prime (p), generator length, generator (g), public value length and public value (g^i mod p). All numbers are binary, most significant byte first.

  • If prime length is 16 or greater, it is the length of p in bytes.
  • If prime length is 1 or 2, the prime field is an unsigned index into a table of 65,536 prime/generator pairs, and the generator length SHOULD be zero.
  • A prime length of zero, or 3 through 15, is reserved.

The corresponding algorithm 2 SIG record is not used, so no format for it is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The record lists the shared numbers and your own public number, each with a length in front. Or, for two popular choices, it just gives a table number instead of spelling the big numbers out.

sections.title: Keeping Records Small
sections.content:
DNS implementations were optimized for small transfers, typically under 512 bytes including overhead. Larger transfers work, and work was underway to make them more efficient, but the RFC advises making reasonable efforts to minimize the size of KEY record sets consistent with adequate security. A secure zone also returns an authenticating SIG record.

The table index form described above is one way to avoid sending a long prime at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book likes short answers, so keep the entries as small as you safely can.

sections.title: Allocating Prime Lengths and Table Entries
sections.content:
Assigning a meaning to prime lengths of 0 and 3 through 15 requires an IETF consensus. The table of well-known prime/generator pairs is split by number range:

  • 0x0000 through 0x07FF: assigned only by an IETF standards action. This document assigns 0x0001 and 0x0002.
  • 0x0800 through 0xBFFF: assignable based on RFC documentation.
  • 0xC000 through 0xFFFF: private use, not centrally coordinated. Using these pairs outside a closed environment may cause conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: The table of ready-made numbers has reserved sections. Some need a formal vote to add, some need a written document, and the last part is free for anyone to use privately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Many of the general security considerations in RFC 2535 apply. Keys retrieved from the DNS should not be trusted unless they were securely obtained from a secure resolver or independently verified by the user, and that process meets the user's security policy. How strong a key must be depends on local policy.

The usual Diffie-Hellman key strength considerations also apply: (p-1)/2 should also be prime, g should be primitive mod p, and p should be large.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trust a key from the phone book if you got it safely. And the shared numbers must be chosen carefully, or the secret is easier to guess.

sections.title: Well-Known Prime Groups (Appendix A)
sections.content:
Appendix A defines the two table entries, copied from the IPSEC effort, where their derivation is explained. Richard Schroeppel did the mathematical and computational work.

  • Group 1: a 768 bit prime, written as 2^768 - 2^704 - 1 + 2^64 * { [2^638 pi] + 149686 }, which is 24 32-bit words long.
  • Group 2: a 1024 bit prime, written as 2^1024 - 2^960 - 1 + 2^64 * { [2^894 pi] + 129093 }, which is 32 32-bit words long.

Both groups use the generator 2, one 32-bit word long.
sections.plainLanguage: Two big shared numbers were worked out ahead of time, so a record can just point to them by table number instead of repeating them.

fields.name: Prime length (or flag)
fields.desc: Length of p in bytes if 16 or greater; 1 or 2 means a table index.
